extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics); readers studying Kant's Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for making and analysing Kantian aesthetic judgements (judgements of taste): what counts as beauty, the basis of pure vs empirical judgements, the role of purposiveness, charm, emotion, concepts, and the Ideal/normal Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty pleases universally without a concept
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beautiful is that which pleases universally, without a concept.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aesthetic judgement claims a satisfaction that is communicable to everyone even though it is not grounded in a concept of the object. Universal validity is asserted on the basis of feeling, not on conceptual cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste rests on the form of purposiveness (no purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The judgement of taste has nothing at its basis but the form of the purposiveness of an object (or of its mode of representation).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste must be determined by the mere form of purposiveness in the representation (a purposiveness without any objective or subjective purpose). If a representation is judged good because of a purpose or interest, it is not a pure judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement is felt (sensation of harmonious play), not intellectual
rubrics_metrics.description: The consciousness of a mutual subjective harmony of the cognitive powers (Imagination and Understanding) in the judgement of taste is known through sensation (the more lively play of both faculties), not by a concept uniting them into cognition of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement arises from the sensation of harmonious mental activity rather than from the application of concepts; if the representation unites Understanding and Imagination into a concept-based cognition, it ceases to be a judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste must be independent of charm and emotion (no interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every interest spoils the judgement of taste and takes from its impartiality... A judgement of taste on which charm and emotion have no influence ... is a pure judgement of taste.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interests, charms, or emotions introduce partiality and empirical grounds that invalidate the claim to universal communicability. Charm may be tolerated as an adjunct but if it becomes the ground of assent it corrupts genuine taste; emotion belongs to sublimity and uses a different standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical (pleasantness) vs pure (beauty/formal) aesthetic judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgements divide into empirical (material) judgements that assert pleasantness and formal (pure) judgements that assert beauty of an object or its manner of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material judgements are judgements of Sense (pleasant/unpleasant) and depend on sensation; formal judgements of Taste concern form and claim universal communicability. Critics must not conflate mere pleasant sensations with beauty proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory qualities count as beautiful only insofar as they are pure form
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours or tones may be called beautiful only in so far as they are 'pure'—a formal determination that admits universal communicability rather than merely contingent sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, pure sensations (e.g., single colours, tones) can be beautiful if uninterfered with by foreign sensations and if their form enables universal communicability. Composite sensations lack this standard and therefore generally do not warrant the predicate 'beautiful' unless their formal role is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be justified by beautiful form; finery that appeals merely by charm injures beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments augment satisfaction only by their form; if ornament is used merely to recommend by charm (like a golden frame used solely to recommend a painting), it is finery and injures genuine beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the formative arts delineation/composition (form) is primary. Decorative elements are permissible only insofar as they clarify or complete the form; otherwise they are extraneous and degrade taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is independent of objective purposiveness (utility) or perfection (good)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful, regarded as formal subjective purposiveness (purposiveness without purpose), is independent of the concept of the Good, which presupposes objective purposiveness (utility or internal perfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judging something beautiful should not be based on its utility or on concepts of what the object ought to be. Confusing beauty with perfection or goodness makes the judgement cognitive rather than aesthetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement is not a cognitive judgement about the object
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste refers the representation to the subject and brings to notice only the purposive form as felt; it gives no cognition (not even a confused cognition) of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judgement purports to describe objective traits or furnish concepts of the object (e.g., internal purpose, perfection), it ceases to be a purely aesthetical judgement. The role of Understanding in taste is not to cognise but to determine representation in relation to felt harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: If beauty is judged under a definite concept (purpose), the judgement is not pure — distinction between free and dependent beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of beauty: free beauty (pulchritudo vaga) presupposes no concept of what the object ought to be; dependent beauty (pulchritudo adhaerens) presupposes such a concept and the object's perfection in accordance with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free beauties (flowers, purely decorative patterns, some music) ground pure judgements of taste. Dependent beauties (human beauty, buildings, animals tied to a use or purpose) involve concepts of purpose and thus contaminate the purity of taste. A pure judgement requires either ignorance of the purpose or deliberate abstraction from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied rules for design are not rules of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: When taste is unified with Reason (beauty subordinated to purpose), it becomes possible to prescribe rules for design, but these are rules for unifying Taste with Reason, not genuine rules of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixing taste by reference to purposes yields objective rules useful for design but they transform an aesthetical judgement into an intellectual or practical one. Evaluators should distinguish between design-rules (applied, purposive) and pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective conceptual rule of taste — universal communicability is empirical/probabilistic via examples
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no objective rule of taste determined by concepts; the empirical criterion (weak) is the agreement, as far as possible, of times and peoples about the feeling produced by certain forms (exemplary models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste cannot be codified into definitive conceptual criteria. Exemplary works may serve as models and help confirm taste empirically, but they do not constitute conceptual rules that determine beauty a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Idea (exemplary average) as a standard: imaginative averaging produces a 'normal Idea' for a species
rubrics_metrics.description: The Imagination can combine many individual images into an average or 'normal Idea' (e.g., the average figure of full-grown men) which serves as an aesthetical standard for the race; this normal Idea pleases by correctness, not by distinctive beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The normal Idea is an imaginative archetype derived from many examples and permits rules for judging correctness within a species or kind. It is not the full archetype of beauty and lacks specific characteristic content; it functions as a correctness-standard rather than as an Ideal containing moral expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of beauty (human) involves moral expression and is not purely aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ideal of beauty applicable only to humans combines an aesthetical normal Idea with a rational Idea (moral purposes). The Ideal consists in visible expression of moral Ideas (goodness, purity, strength, peace) in bodily manifestation and thus is not a mere pure judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgements that appeal to an Ideal incorporating moral ideas go beyond pure aesthetics; they produce interest and sustained satisfaction but are partly intellectual/practical. Evaluators should note when moral expressiveness, not mere form, is the ground of approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitional formulation: Beauty is form of purposiveness without representation of a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: “Beauty is the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concise formula encapsulates the core criterion: the perceived purposiveness (fit of form to cognitive faculties) must occur without thinking of an objective or subjective purpose. All legitimate uses, examples, and exclusions in Kant's account elaborate this central condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality: the beautiful is thought as having necessary reference to satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is thought as having a necessary reference to satisfaction (i.e., we think the beautiful as necessarily related to a feeling of pleasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant treats the modality of aesthetic judgement as claiming necessity or universal validity for the satisfaction it asserts. Evaluators should be attentive to the claim that an aesthetic judgement asks assent as if the pleasure were necessary and communicable to others.
